verses.context: Mocked by arrogant people for his loyalty to God's law, the writer of Psalm 119 reaches back past his own troubles to much older memories.

KJV.displayText: I thought on my ways, and turned my feet unto thy testimonies.

CPDV.displayText: I have considered my ways, and I have turned my feet toward your testimonies.

verses.context: In a stanza that begins by calling the Lord his portion, the Psalm 119 writer recalls a moment of honest self-examination.

KJV.text: How many are the days of thy servant? when wilt thou execute judgment on them that persecute me?
KJV.displayText: How many are the days of thy servant? when wilt thou execute judgment on them that persecute me?

BSB.displayText: How many days must Your servant wait? When will You execute judgment on my persecutors?

CPDV.displayText: How many are the days of your servant? When will you bring judgment against those who persecute me?

verses.context: Feeling like a wineskin shriveled in the smoke, the writer of Psalm 119 turns from his own weariness to the arrogant men who are hunting him.

KJV.text: Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers: the snare is broken, and we are escaped.
KJV.displayText: Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers: the snare is broken, and we are escaped.

CPDV.displayText: Our soul has been snatched away like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters. The snare has been broken, and we have been freed.

verses.context: Imagining how enemies could have swallowed Israel alive had the Lord not been on their side, David blesses God for not handing his people over as prey.

KJV.text: For the Lord hath chosen Jacob unto himself, and Israel for his peculiar treasure.
KJV.displayText: For the Lord hath chosen Jacob unto himself, and Israel for his peculiar treasure.

CPDV.displayText: For the Lord has chosen Jacob for himself, Israel for his own possession.

verses.context: Calling the servants who stand in the temple courts to sing praise, the psalm's writer grounds that praise in God's choice of his people.

KJV.text: Surely the righteous shall give thanks unto thy name: the upright shall dwell in thy presence.
KJV.displayText: Surely the righteous shall give thanks unto thy name: the upright shall dwell in thy presence.

BSB.displayText: Surely the righteous will praise Your name; the upright will dwell in Your presence.

CPDV.displayText: So then, truly, the just will confess your name, and the upright will dwell with your countenance.

verses.context: David ends this plea for rescue from slanderers and violent men on a note of settled confidence about the future of the upright.

KJV.text: But mine eyes are unto thee, O God the Lord: in thee is my trust; leave not my soul destitute.
KJV.displayText: But mine eyes are unto thee, O God the Lord: in thee is my trust; leave not my soul destitute.

BSB.displayText: But my eyes are fixed on You, O GOD the Lord. In You I seek refuge; do not leave my soul defenseless.

CPDV.displayText: For Lord, O Lord, my eyes look to you. In you, I have hoped. Do not take away my soul.

verses.context: Asking God to guard his mouth and keep him from the company of evildoers, David turns his attention from his enemies' traps to the Lord himself.

KJV.displayText: Deliver me, O Lord, from mine enemies: I flee unto thee to hide me.

BSB.displayText: Deliver me from my enemies, O LORD; I flee to You for refuge.

CPDV.text: O Lord, rescue me from my enemies. I have fled to you.
CPDV.displayText: O Lord, rescue me from my enemies. I have fled to you.

verses.context: With his spirit failing and enemies pressing him, David stops recalling God's past deeds and asks plainly for rescue and shelter.

KJV.text: Man is like to vanity: his days are as a shadow that passeth away.
KJV.displayText: Man is like to vanity: his days are as a shadow that passeth away.

BSB.displayText: Man is like a breath; his days are like a passing shadow.

CPDV.displayText: Man has been made similar to vanity. His days pass by like a shadow.

verses.context: In a psalm that opens by praising God for training his hands for battle, David stops to ask why the Lord pays any attention to people at all.

KJV.text: The eyes of all wait upon thee; and thou givest them their meat in due season.
KJV.displayText: The eyes of all wait upon thee; and thou givest them their meat in due season.

BSB.displayText: The eyes of all look to You, and You give them their food in season.

CPDV.displayText: O Lord, all eyes hope in you, and you provide their food in due time.

verses.context: Having praised the Lord as a King whose rule lasts through all generations, David turns to the ordinary way this King cares for his realm day by day.

KJV.text: He maketh peace in thy borders, and filleth thee with the finest of the wheat.
KJV.displayText: He maketh peace in thy borders, and filleth thee with the finest of the wheat.

BSB.displayText: He makes peace at your borders; He fills you with the finest wheat.

CPDV.displayText: He has stationed peace at your borders, and he has satisfied you with the fat of the grain.

verses.context: Addressing Jerusalem, whose scattered exiles God has gathered home, the psalm's writer describes the security and plenty God gives the city.

KJV.text: Yea, in the way of thy judgments, O Lord, have we waited for thee; the desire of our soul is to thy name, and to the remembrance of thee.
KJV.displayText: Yea, in the way of thy judgments, O Lord, have we waited for thee; the desire of our soul is to thy name, and to the remembrance of thee.

BSB.displayText: Yes, we wait for You, O LORD; we walk in the path of Your judgments. Your name and renown are the desire of our souls.

CPDV.displayText: And in the path of your judgments, O Lord, we have endured for you. Your name and your remembrance are the desire of the soul.

verses.context: Voicing a faithful people who have watched God humble a proud city, Isaiah describes their patient waiting and the deepest desire of their hearts.

KJV.text: With my soul have I desired thee in the night; yea, with my spirit within me will I seek thee early: for when thy judgments are in the earth, the inhabitants of the world will learn righteousness.

BSB.displayText: My soul longs for You in the night; indeed, my spirit seeks You at dawn. For when Your judgments come upon the earth, the people of the world learn righteousness.

CPDV.displayText: My soul has desired you in the night. But I will also watch for you with my spirit, in my inmost heart, from the morning. When you accomplish your judgments upon the earth, the inhabitants of the world will learn justice.

verses.context: Where the song before this line spoke for a whole waiting people, Isaiah now shifts to the first person and to the hours when he prays.

KJV.text: The meek also shall increase their joy in the Lord, and the poor among men shall rejoice in the Holy One of Israel.
KJV.displayText: The meek also shall increase their joy in the Lord, and the poor among men shall rejoice in the Holy One of Israel.

BSB.displayText: The humble will increase their joy in the LORD, and the poor among men will rejoice in the Holy One of Israel.

CPDV.displayText: And the meek will increase their rejoicing in the Lord, and the poor among men will exult in the Holy One of Israel.

verses.context: After condemning people who hide their schemes from God, Isaiah looks ahead to a day when the deaf will hear and the blind will see.

KJV.text: For the Lord is our judge, the Lord is our lawgiver, the Lord is our king; he will save us.
KJV.displayText: For the Lord is our judge, the Lord is our lawgiver, the Lord is our king; he will save us.

BSB.displayText: For the LORD is our Judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our King. It is He who will save us.

CPDV.displayText: For the Lord is our judge. The Lord is our lawgiver. The Lord is our king. He himself will save us.

verses.context: Looking ahead to a Jerusalem free of foreign invaders, Isaiah pictures the city as a quiet, secure home with God himself as its protector.

KJV.text: I have not spoken in secret, in a dark place of the earth: I said not unto the seed of Jacob, Seek ye me in vain: I the Lord speak righteousness, I declare things that are right.

BSB.displayText: I have not spoken in secret, from a place in a land of darkness. I did not say to the descendants of Jacob, ‘Seek Me in a wasteland.’ I, the LORD, speak the truth; I say what is right.

verses.context: Setting God, the maker of heaven and earth, against the idols of the nations, Isaiah relays how God describes the way he has spoken to Israel.

KJV.displayText: Who hath believed our report? and to whom is the arm of the Lord revealed?

CPDV.displayText: Who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?

verses.context: Near the start of Isaiah's song about God's suffering servant, the prophet wonders aloud who could believe what he is about to describe.

KJV.displayText: He shall see of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied: by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many; for he shall bear their iniquities.

CPDV.displayText: Because his soul has labored, he will see and be satisfied. By his knowledge, my just servant will himself justify many, and he himself will carry their iniquities.

verses.context: Having described the servant's silent suffering and unjust death, Isaiah now gives God's own verdict on what that suffering will achieve.

KJV.text: Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not? hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness.
KJV.displayText: Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not? hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness.

BSB.displayText: Why spend money on that which is not bread, and your labor on that which does not satisfy? Listen carefully to Me, and eat what is good, and your soul will delight in the richest of foods.

CPDV.displayText: Why do you spend money for what is not bread, and expend your labor for what does not satisfy? Listen very closely to me, and eat what is good, and then your soul will be delighted by a full measure.

verses.context: Like a market vendor calling to passersby, God speaks through Isaiah to people wearing themselves out on things that leave them empty.

KJV.text: Even unto them will I give in mine house and within my walls a place and a name better than of sons and of daughters: I will give them an everlasting name, that shall not be cut off.
KJV.displayText: Even unto them will I give in mine house and within my walls a place and a name better than of sons and of daughters: I will give them an everlasting name, that shall not be cut off.

BSB.displayText: I will give them, in My house and within My walls, a memorial and a name better than that of sons and daughters. I will give them an everlasting name that will not be cut off.

CPDV.displayText: I will give them a place in my house, within my walls, and a name better than sons and daughters. I will give them an everlasting name, which will never perish.

verses.context: Addressing eunuchs who felt shut out of God's people because they could have no children, Isaiah brings a promise for all who hold to God's covenant.

KJV.text: Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke?

BSB.displayText: Isn’t this the fast that I have chosen: to break the chains of wickedness, to untie the cords of the yoke, to set the oppressed free and tear off every yoke?

CPDV.displayText: Is not this, instead, the kind of fast that I have chosen? Release the constraints of impiety; relieve the burdens that oppress; freely forgive those who are broken; and break apart every burden.

verses.context: When people complain that God ignores their fasting, God answers through Isaiah by describing the kind of fast he actually wants.

KJV.text: Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him; and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh?
KJV.displayText: Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him; and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh?

CPDV.displayText: Break your bread with the hungry, and lead the destitute and the homeless into your house. When you see someone naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh.

verses.context: Continuing God's reply to people who fasted while mistreating their workers, Isaiah moves from breaking chains to everyday acts of care close to home.

KJV.text: Violence shall no more be heard in thy land, wasting nor destruction within thy borders; but thou shalt call thy walls Salvation, and thy gates Praise.

BSB.displayText: No longer will violence be heard in your land, nor ruin or destruction within your borders. But you will name your walls Salvation and your gates Praise.

CPDV.displayText: Iniquity will no longer be heard in your land, nor devastation and destruction in your borders. And salvation will occupy your walls, and praise will occupy your gates.

verses.context: Speaking to a Zion that had long been forsaken and despised, Isaiah promises that God will one day make the city a place of lasting safety.

verses.context: Speaking for a people whose sanctuary has been trampled by enemies, Isaiah dares to ask God why he has let them wander from his ways.

verses.context: After calming Jeremiah's fear of speaking, God gives the young prophet a physical sign to mark the start of his work.
